p.x:
Yesterday, I went to get a haircut. My hair was very long and curly, and it was hard to comb in the morning. My mum said, "It's time for a change!"
I went to a small shop near my house. The man washed my hair with shampoo and then cut it short. It only took twenty minutes. Now my hair is easy to look after.
While I was there, an old man came in. He had a long white beard, and he asked the barber to shave it off! After that, a girl came in to get her nails cleaned at the shop next door. I like my new haircut. My friends say it looks cool.

Many people spend a lot of time and money on their appearance. Some women wear make-up every day, with lipstick and a little perfume, while others prefer a natural look. Men, too, are paying more attention to how they look. Many visit a barber regularly, and some have a skincare routine.
Going to the salon is popular in Thailand. A good hairdresser can cut, style or dye your hair. Some people choose long, straight hair; others prefer a ponytail or short hair. Tattoos and piercings are also more common than in the past, especially among young people.
In hot countries, sunscreen is the most important product. Some people want to look tanned, but too much sun can damage skin and cause wrinkles. The cosmetics industry sells creams for every problem!
Fashion is also big business. Every season, designers show new clothes on the catwalk in Paris, Milan and New York. However, fast fashion, cheap clothes made quickly to follow trends, creates huge amounts of waste. Many people now prefer to buy fewer, better-quality clothes. Whatever your style, remember: the most handsome or gorgeous person isn't always the one who looks slim and perfect, but the one who feels confident.

The global beauty industry is worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and its influence on how people see themselves is enormous. Every culture has its own beauty standards, and these standards change over time. In much of East and Southeast Asia, for example, a pale complexion has long been considered attractive, and whitening creams fill the shelves of pharmacies. In parts of Europe, by contrast, a tanned look was once fashionable as a sign of holidays and wealth.
Critics argue that the industry profits from insecurity. Advertisements feature models with flawless skin, often airbrushed to remove every imperfection, and promote anti-ageing products that promise to stop time. Constant exposure to such images, particularly on social media, can damage self-image, especially among young people. In some countries, cosmetic surgery has become so common that it is almost seen as normal for young adults.
At the other end of the market lies the world of luxury. Haute couture, handmade garments produced by elite fashion houses in Paris, can cost as much as a car, and wealthy clients order bespoke suits and dresses that fit them perfectly. Such items represent craftsmanship and artistry, but also a level of spending that many find difficult to justify.
Yet caring about appearance is not simply vanity. For many people, choosing clothes, make-up or a hairstyle is a form of self-expression and creativity. The challenge, many psychologists suggest, is to enjoy beauty without allowing it to define our worth.
